about: Written by `bin/console app:policies:import` (omnisense/contracts' PolicyExport): each provider's policy.json at its published head (ref). Edit the package's file, never this one.

provenance.notes: XP Z12-013 is the API standard every approved platform (plateforme agréée) exposes; the rights, limits and prices are each platform's, in its contract with the company, and none is declared here. A site tightens this policy with its platform's figures (the gateway's 'policy' option). The Flow Service takes files of 100 MB at most.

Limits unknown: PISTE's terms (3.1.3) say the AIFE sets each API's usage limits at its discretion and documents them with the API, on the PISTE portal behind an account; none is published openly, so none is declared. Commercial: the terms define an application as one exploiting the APIs 'for commercial purposes or not'. The API key (a PISTE application's client id and secret) must not be shared outside the organisation (3.1.2), and every call also needs a Chorus Pro technical account. The portal's content may not be redistributed without the AIFE's authorisation (2.7), which does not cover the data the APIs return; each API may carry terms of its own. Chorus Pro's own terms (the policy address) did not load on 2026-11-10. Price: not stated in the terms read.

No API: the invoice leaves through the application's own mailer (symfony/mailer), so there are no provider terms. The sending limits are the mail server's or the transactional e-mail provider's: a site declares them with the gateway's 'policy' option (operations: submit). Legal for a small company's invoices until it must issue through an approved platform (1 September 2027 for SMEs and micro-companies).

Limits unknown: Odoo's external API reference states no rate limit nor quota (Odoo Online databases have been seen answering 429, no figure published); a self-hosted database's limits are its own. Commercial declared as 'contract': on Odoo Online the external API is only available on the Custom pricing plan (not One App Free nor Standard); a self-hosted Community edition is free. An API key is a user's, lasts three months at most (rotate it), up to 10 keys a user programmatically. XML-RPC and JSON-RPC are removed in Odoo 22 (fall 2028) / Online 21.1 (winter 2027); this package calls JSON-2 (/json/2). Storage, caching and redistribution: the reference does not say.

rateLimits.note: 25 requests every 5 seconds per token (a developer token, or each token of an OAuth app), every endpoint, production and sandbox alike; a 429 carries retry-after, every answer ratelimit-limit, -remaining and -reset (a Unix time)

provenance.notes: Commercial: the licence is for the company's own internal business purposes (contract terms 2.1); an integration serving several Pennylane customers needs API Partner status and an OAuth app from Pennylane (2.1 d, 3.1). Storage declared as 'contract': no copy or database of the data beyond what the intended integration needs (3.4 p), data returned or deleted on termination as users instruct (9.5). Redistribution, resale and sublicensing of the API forbidden (3.4 f); no competing service, no suggested affiliation (3.4 m, o); Pennylane may set and change limits at its discretion (3.4 c, 3.5) and is granted a licence over the integrations (4.3). No attribution required. Price: no API price in the terms; a company API token needs Pennylane's Essential plan or above. Caching: the terms set no duration.

CalDAV is a protocol: each server's own terms and limits apply, and the site configures them (policy). Read on 2026-11-10: iCloud (https://caldav.icloud.com/, which answers from a pNN-caldav.icloud.com partition) needs an app-specific password, which needs two-factor authentication, at most 25 active, all revoked when the Apple Account password changes (https://support.apple.com/en-us/102654); Apple publishes no CalDAV developer terms nor limits. Fastmail (https://caldav.fastmail.com/) needs an app password, and its Basic plan has no CalDAV (https://www.fastmail.help/hc/en-us/articles/1500000278342); no limits documented. Nextcloud (https://<host>/remote.php/dav) throttles failed logins, no read limit documented. Google's CalDAV (https://apidata.googleusercontent.com/caldav/v2/) takes OAuth 2.0 only and shares the Calendar API's quotas (10,000 requests a minute per project, 600 a minute per user; https://developers.google.com/workspace/calendar/api/guides/quota): a site using it tightens this policy with them. The free-busy-query REPORT (RFC 4791 §7.10) is not supported by Google (its CalDAV guide) and reported unsupported by iCloud: busy time is then computed from the events of the span.

rateLimits.note: Calendar API: 10,000 requests a minute per Google Cloud project (sliding window), since 2026-05-01; projects that used the API between November 2025 and April 2026 keep their former quotas. Over it Google answers 403 or 429 (usageLimits: rateLimitExceeded).
600 requests a minute per user per project (sliding window): 403 userRateLimitExceeded over it. Count it per user: Registry::calendarEvents($name, $user).
1,000,000 requests a day per project is the threshold before charges apply and cannot be raised; Google announced charges beyond it for later in 2026, with 90 days' notice at least.

provenance.notes: Commercial use is not forbidden by the Google APIs Terms of Service; no sublicensing, no substitute for the API, no circumventing the limits. Caching is left unknown: the terms forbid keeping API content beyond what its cache headers allow (§5(e)), while a user's own events are user data under the Google API Services User Data Policy, which sets no time to live. Storage is allowed for the user-facing feature the user consented to, under Limited Use (https://developers.google.com/terms/api-services-user-data-policy): secured in transit and at rest, no transfer but the listed exceptions, no human reading without the user's agreement, no ads; deleted when the terms end (§8(b)). Redistribution is forbidden (no sublicensing, no transfer of user data). No attribution is required; the branding rules apply: say "for" or "compatible with" Google Calendar with a trademark notice, never use the mark as the site's name or logo. Calendar scopes are sensitive: an external app needs Google's verification (a privacy policy, a home page, a verified domain, a justification per scope, a demo video); an unverified app is capped at 100 new users, and an app in Testing status gets refresh tokens that last 7 days. A refresh token also dies unused for 6 months, when the user revokes access, or past 100 per account per client.

rateLimits.note: Outlook's limit: 10,000 API requests in any 10 minutes per app and mailbox, with 4 requests at a time and 150 MB uploaded (PATCH, POST, PUT) per 5 minutes; counted per user (mailbox). Above it Graph answers 429 with Retry-After, which the client honours. The global limit is 130,000 requests per 10 seconds per app across all tenants.

provenance.notes: Microsoft APIs Terms of Use (last updated October 2025): a limited, revocable licence for applications offered to customers, no ban on commercial use (Microsoft may set fees or limits at any time). Ask for the minimum data and permissions; no copies or databases of the data beyond what the intended scenario needs; Outlook data without further consent only to sync or back up calendar events; data kept locally stays current (corrections and deletions mirrored), has retention and deletion rules, and is deleted when the user leaves; a privacy statement as protective as Microsoft's; no advertising use; no redistribution, resale or sublicensing of the APIs or the data (§14); no circumvention of limits. Caching and storage are marked allowed under those conditions. Permissions: Calendars.Read to read, Calendars.ReadWrite to write, offline_access for a refresh token; getSchedule's pages disagree (Calendars.ReadBasic in the reference, Calendars.Read in the concept page): Calendars.Read holds under both. getSchedule is for work or school accounts only, not personal Microsoft accounts.

"For commercial purposes we require active sponsorship" (https://github.com/sponsors/nager): commercial use is by agreement (a site says usage: {commercial: true, contract: true} once it sponsors). "It is not allowed to use the holiday information to publish or operate your own holiday portal" (redistribution forbidden). The API page says no rate limits and unlimited queries (rateLimits: none). The terms (last updated 2023-09-15) say nothing on attribution, caching or storage; the answers carry Cache-Control: public, max-age=604800. Nager.Date moved from date.nager.at to nagerholidays.com; this package calls API v4 (/api/v4/Holidays/{country}/{year}): v3 ends on 2027-01-31. v4 names holidays in English only, and its subdivisionCodes are ISO 3166-2. The Docker image and the NuGet package need a licence key (sponsors get one); base_uri points at a self-hosted instance. An unknown country is a 404 (no holiday here).

Free of charge and allowed in commercial projects (the FAQ). The data is under the Open Database License 1.0: credit the source, and a database made from it is shared under the same licence; the server is AGPL-3.0 and can be self-hosted (base_uri). No rate limit, caching rule nor User-Agent rule is stated anywhere (rateLimits null: unknown); this package sends the site's User-Agent when one is given. validFrom and validTo may be at most three years apart (each call here asks for one calendar year). An unknown country is answered with an empty list. Regions are OpenHolidays' subdivision codes: ISO 3166-2 where the country has them (DE-BY), the API's own otherwise (FR-GE-BR, FR-GE-HR and FR-GE-MO for Alsace and Moselle, DE-BY-AU for the city of Augsburg). 36 countries; BR, SE and VA have public holidays only.

rateLimits.note: 60 requests a second per API resource by default (400 a second to run an actor); 250,000 a minute per user overall. Over it Apify answers 429 rate-limit-exceeded, with no Retry-After documented: back off exponentially from 500 ms.

provenance.notes: General terms effective 2026-07-09, for business use only. §5.8: the customer is solely responsible for the legality, accuracy, quality, appropriateness and use of all Customer Data; Apify may delete it after termination (§15.6). The acceptable use policy (2026-02-20) bans activities that contravene applicable laws or the rights of any third party, and putting an undue burden on any servers. Neither mentions robots.txt. Limits: https://docs.apify.com/api/v2 (rate limiting). Each run also costs compute units of the account's plan. Not used: Apify Proxy (residential or datacenter groups), retries, link following, sitemaps, browser actors.

rateLimits.note: /scrape, per team: the free plan's figure, the default; the "plan" option picks another (plans).
Free plan: /crawl 2 requests a minute per team, which batch scrape shares; counted on starting a run (the status reads are not in the published table read on that day).

provenance.notes: Terms revised 2026-10-07. §5.d.1 forbids use for commercial purposes except as expressly authorized by Firecrawl: declared "contract" (a paid plan's agreement is that authorization; check yours). §7.g: use only in compliance with all applicable laws and regulations; the customer indemnifies Firecrawl and accepts all risks associated with third parties and their content - the legality of collecting a site stays the site's operator's, which is why omnicrawl's gate decides before Firecrawl is called. The terms say nothing of robots.txt or of keeping results. Limits are per team and per plan (https://docs.firecrawl.dev/rate-limits): this policy's figures are the free plan's, the default; plans declares hobby, standard, growth and scale, picked with the factory's "plan" option; a 429 covers rate and concurrency, with Retry-After when available. Firecrawl checks robots.txt itself for the token FirecrawlAgent and * before crawling, which the family does not rely on. Not used: proxy "enhanced"/"auto" (anti-bot proxies), actions, location, mobile.

provenance.notes: Terms updated 2024-07-15. §10: the user is solely responsible that each scraping operation is authorised by the target's terms; §6 forbids breaching the terms of use of third-party websites, and asks for ScrapingBee's prior authorisation when in doubt - which is the gate's job before ScrapingBee is called. §6 also bans use "in a commercial manner" in a wording that reads ambiguously next to paid plans: declared unknown. User data is deleted on termination (§9). No rate per time is published; plans limit concurrent requests (25 on the cheapest, Hobby; the trial's 1,000 credits state none) and a 429 means too many concurrent requests (not billed, no Retry-After documented). Every request goes out through ScrapingBee's rotating proxy pool, with no switch to turn it off: the target cannot tell who collects from the address it sees. omnicrawl therefore uses ScrapingBee, as Zyte API, for targets declared as one's own site or with written permission only; it asks for no premium or stealth proxy and for the target's status as it is (transparent_status_code), which turns off the retry through another proxy. Concurrency per plan: plans (https://www.scrapingbee.com/pricing/); this policy's figure is the default plan's (Hobby).

hobby.note: The cheapest plan with a published concurrency (the free trial states none). No rate per time is published for any plan.

rateLimits.note: 3,000 requests a minute per API key on the standard plans; Zyte also applies per-site and per-account-site limits it does not publish (429 /limits/over-domain-limit, /limits/over-org-domain-limit).

provenance.notes: Terms of 2026-09-22. §3.4: it is up to the customer to determine the legality of the way it uses the services; use for internal business purposes; Zyte may suspend a customer who breached the terms of a targeted data source. The acceptable use policy bans illegal collection, personal data in breach of data-protection law, sites whose terms the customer agreed to and that forbid it, LinkedIn, use that materially interferes with a website's normal operations, and AI uses prohibited or high-risk under the EU AI Act. No robots.txt clause. Rate: https://docs.zyte.com/zyte-api/usage/rate-limit.html; 429s are free and to be retried with exponential backoff (about 20-40 s at first); 520 is a temporary ban, 521 a permanent one (https://docs.zyte.com/zyte-api/usage/errors.html). Ban avoidance (CAPTCHA handling, residential IPs) is on by default and cannot be turned off per request: omnicrawl uses Zyte for targets declared as one's own site or with written permission only.

rateLimits.note: "The global rate limit for the Cloudflare API is 1,200 requests per five minute period per user", shared by the dashboard, API keys and API tokens: counted here for the whole application, the stricter form (several tokens of one user share it). Past it, every call is refused with a 429 for the next five minutes.
Client API per IP: 200 a second (counted for the whole application, the stricter form).

provenance.notes: The limits page (read 2026-11-10) gives 1,200 requests per 5 minutes per user and 200 a second per IP; Enterprise customers may ask Support for more. Cloudflare answers Ratelimit and Ratelimit-Policy fields and a Retry-After on a 429; this provider goes through cloudflare/sdk's Guzzle adapter, so only a 429's fields are read (successful answers' headers are not exposed by the SDK). A call is one operation: records() follows the pages (100 records each) inside one operation, so a large zone spends more requests than the guard counts. The Self-Serve Subscription Agreement (last updated 2025-09-12) does not address commercial use, caching or storage of what the API answers; it forbids circumventing Service-specific usage limits (2.2.1(c)) and selling access to the Services to a third party (2.2.1(a)). Not a data source: rights unknown rather than guessed.

rateLimits.note: "1000 requests per minute from the same IP address" (API reference): counted for the whole application, the stricter form when it runs on several addresses.

provenance.notes: The API reference (read 2026-11-10) gives 1,000 requests per minute per source IP and no status or header for it; a 429 and its Retry-After are honoured when Gandi sends them. The contracts page lists the General Terms (MSA 2020.1.1), the Reseller contract and the OAuth 2.0 special conditions as PDFs; none of them is read here for an API usage clause, so commercial use, caching and storage are unknown. A personal access token is required. The sandbox (api.sandbox.gandi.net) is a separate account.

OVHcloud publishes no rate limit for its core API (eu.api.ovh.com: /domain, /order) as of 2026-11-10; the limits it documents (20 requests a second per project, 60 a minute on Keystone) are the Public Cloud OpenStack APIs', not this one: unknown, not declared. A 429 is honoured (Guzzle's exception carries the answer). The application key, secret and consumer key are required. Terms: OVHcloud's general and specific conditions; nothing read on what an API answer may be used for.

Scaleway publishes no rate limit for its Domains and DNS API as of 2026-11-10 (the rate limits it documents are the Generative APIs'; the API reference answered 403 to the reading); unknown, not declared. A 429 and its Retry-After are honoured. A secret key (X-Auth-Token) is required. Nothing read on what an API answer may be used for: rights unknown.

rateLimits.note: ImportTerminology: 5 transactions a second
GetTerminology: 10 transactions a second
ListTerminologies: 10 transactions a second
DeleteTerminology: 5 transactions a second

provenance.notes: Read on 2026-11-10. Limits: the terminology calls' rates are declared; TranslateText's and TranslateDocument's are not published. A text holds at most 10,000 bytes (UTF-8), a document 100 KB and 100,000 characters, English on one side; 100 terminologies a region (adjustable), 20 MB each, 256 terms used by TranslateText, one terminology a translation. Throttling answers 400 (TooManyRequestsException), not 429: a ProviderException the registry falls back past. Free tier: 2,000,000 characters a month of standard text translation for 12 months from the first request; none for real-time document translation. No plans are declared: the quotas page (read again on 2026-11-10) states the same quotas for every account, with no tier, and the free tier is a price for the first year, not a limit the API applies. Attribution: not required; AWS suggests attributing translations to machine translation. Data retention: Amazon may store and use text inputs to provide, maintain and improve Amazon Translate and other Amazon machine-learning technologies, possibly in another region; an AWS Organizations AI services opt-out policy stops it, and AWS Support deletes what was stored on request. Commercial use: no restriction stated in the pages read, hence unknown.

rateLimits.note: F0 (free): 2,000,000 characters an hour (text translation, standard models), to be consumed evenly through the hour

provenance.notes: Read on 2026-11-10. Limits: no request count is limited ('There are no limits on concurrent requests'); characters are, per hour and by tier - F0 (free) 2,000,000 an hour, to be used evenly (about 33,300 a minute), S1 and multi-service 40,000,000, S2/C2 40,000,000, S3/C3 120,000,000, S4/C4 200,000,000; a request holds at most 1,000 texts and 50,000 characters (detection: 100 texts); a synchronous document at most 10 MB, 6,000,000 characters a minute. Out of quota: 429; a spent free trial: 403. Declared per tier in plans (f0 the default; s1, multi-service, s2, c2, s3, c3, s4, c4), counted in characters translated per subscription key; the factory's "plan" option names the resource's tier. Detection, dictionary and document translation are not counted (the page states no hourly figure for them; synchronous documents: 6,000,000 characters a minute on every tier). Data retention: text translation does not store customer data; document translation stores it while it works, then deletes it for good. Commercial use and attribution: the pages read do not state them, hence unknown and not required. The free tier's monthly amount was not read (only the hourly limits above).

rateLimits.note: F0 (free): 2,000,000 characters an hour (text translation, standard models), to be consumed evenly through the hour

f0.note: The free tier, the default: about 33,300 characters a minute when spread evenly, as the page says.

rateLimits.note: S1: 40,000,000 characters an hour (text translation, standard models), to be consumed evenly through the hour
Multi-service (as S1): 40,000,000 characters an hour (text translation, standard models), to be consumed evenly through the hour

multi-service.note: The page: limits for multi-service subscriptions are the same as the S1 tier.

rateLimits.note: S2: 40,000,000 characters an hour (text translation, standard models), to be consumed evenly through the hour
C2: 40,000,000 characters an hour (text translation, standard models), to be consumed evenly through the hour
S3: 120,000,000 characters an hour (text translation, standard models), to be consumed evenly through the hour
C3: 120,000,000 characters an hour (text translation, standard models), to be consumed evenly through the hour
S4: 200,000,000 characters an hour (text translation, standard models), to be consumed evenly through the hour
C4: 200,000,000 characters an hour (text translation, standard models), to be consumed evenly through the hour

provenance.notes: Read on 2026-11-10 (terms 'Last update: August 2026'). Limits: no request rate is published; DeepL answers 429 (wait, then retry: honoured by the guard) and 456 when the plan's character quota is spent (a ProviderException with status 456, never retried). A request holds at most 128 KiB, headers 16 KiB; documents are billed at least 50,000 characters each. Quotas are in characters per plan, and no plan is declared: on 2026-11-10 the API plans page (support.deepl.com, DeepL API plans) answered 403, the pricing page draws its API tab by script, and the usage-limits page gives no per-plan figure; the account's own limit is what GET /v2/usage answers (character_limit), which a site declares as its tightening (policy: unit characters, operation translate). Plans: DeepL API Free and Pro are no longer sold to new accounts; Developer (free of charge), Growth and Enterprise are. Commercial use: allowed under the terms, for the customer's own purposes (§8.1.1), not to build a competing product or API (§8.1.1(f), §8.1.9). Attribution: an application shown to end users must tell them the output is DeepL's, with DeepL's logo or name including its domain (§8.3.3). Data retention: content stored only as technically required (§3.1.2), encrypted for debugging at most 72 hours (§3.1.4), never used to train DeepL's models on paid plans; on DeepL API Developer, DeepL may store content perpetually (§3.3.2) and no personal data may be processed (§8.3.11). Caching and storage of translations: the terms read say nothing, hence unknown.

rateLimits.note: v3 requests per project per minute (a default quota, raised on request in the Cloud console)
requests for the supported languages per project per minute, v2 and v3 together

characters sent to the general model per project per minute, v2 and v3 together, whitespace included; detectLanguage counts too (a custom model has 100,000 of its own, which a site using one declares)

provenance.notes: Read on 2026-11-10 (docs.cloud.google.com, where cloud.google.com/translate/docs now redirects). Limits: besides the request quotas, 6,000,000 characters a minute per project to the general model (v2 and v3 together, detection included: declared in characters; 100,000 to a custom model, counted apart), 2,400 document pages a minute, 30,000 code points a request (v3); a quota exceeded answers 403 (User Rate Limit Exceeded), not 429. Attribution: required - the 'powered by Google Translate' graphic adjacent to every translation, linked to http://translate.google.com; a page that can be indexed marks machine-translated text as such; the product's name may not hold Google's brands. Data retention: content held briefly in memory to translate it, used for nothing but the service, never to train Google's translation; glossaries stored, encrypted, on Google Cloud. Keys: v3 takes no API key, only OAuth 2.0 tokens (a service account or Application Default Credentials). Pricing and its free tier: the pricing page could not be read on 2026-11-10, so no figure is declared. Commercial use: a Google Cloud service under its terms; caching and storage of translations: the pages read say nothing, hence unknown.

Read on 2026-11-10, for a server the site runs itself: LibreTranslate is software (AGPL-3.0, API 1.9.6), not a service with terms, so its limits and rights are the operator's - none by default (--req-limit, --char-limit, --batch-limit: 'No limit'; --api-keys: disabled). A site that starts its server with limits writes them in its policy option, so that the guard counts them; the server answers 429 ('Slow down') beyond them. AGPL-3.0 binds whoever modifies and serves LibreTranslate itself, not an application calling its API. Data retention: a self-hosted server's is its operator's (nothing in the docs read says it keeps texts). Storage and redistribution of translations: they come from Argos Translate's language models, whose licences were not read, hence unknown. libretranslate.com, the public instance, is not this policy: it needs a paid key (Pro: bursts of 80 a minute, 2,000 characters a call; Business: 200 a minute), does not store or log texts, keeps IP addresses and keys 2 days against abuse; its mirrors say nothing of programmatic use, so no live call is made from this package's tests.

The site's own Docker Engine, over its unix socket or TCP: no rate limit, the containers and their data are the site's. Docker Engine is under the Apache License 2.0. Docker Desktop is not: its Subscription Service Agreement (updated August 26, 2026) asks a paid subscription for commercial use in businesses of more than 250 employees or more than US$10 million in annual revenue, and of government entities. Access to the socket amounts to root on the host; remote access without TLS is not recommended.

rateLimits.note: "Deployments at 40 requests per second", per organization: start's POST /v2/deployments. Start then reads GET /v1/status/{request_id} until the server has an address: "Context & Status at 20 requests per second", requests made inside one start, which the guard does not count one by one. stop (DELETE /v1/stop/{request_id}) and running (GET /v1/deployments) are named in neither: not counted.

provenance.notes: A paid service: its pay-as-you-go Standard Terms (or a subscription's) are the contract; they bar its competitors and any monitoring or benchmarking use. The API token (Authorization: token ...) gives unlimited access to the account: never in a game client. Caching, storage, credit: not stated. Edgegap asks to be contacted before releases and load tests.

GOG publishes no API nor developer terms for api.gog.com and catalog.gog.com (docs.gog.com covers the GALAXY SDK for publishers only; gogapidocs.readthedocs.io is a community's). Its User Agreement (effective 9 March 2026) asks, 11.1(e), not to create or use "automation software, robots, bots, spiders, scripts, extraction tools or other software that interact with or affect GOG services or GOG content in any way", unauthorized third-party programs collecting information about GOG services included: whoever runs this provider should ask GOG first. Limits, rights and credit are not stated. api.gog.com answers cache-control: max-age=86400 (observed, not a policy).

rateLimits.note: "There is a rate limit of 4 requests per second", answered by 429 beyond it; and "up to 8 open requests at any moment in time" (concurrency). Twitch's application token, asked of id.twitch.tv, is one request more when it is renewed.

provenance.notes: IGDB is free for non-commercial use under the Twitch Developer Services Agreement; its FAQ says the API is free for commercial projects too, but monetized products go through its commercial partnership (partner@igdb.com), and the Agreement forbids selling, licensing or monetizing Twitch Data without Twitch's written permission: commercial use is declared under contract. Storage and caching: IGDB's FAQ "we prefer if you store and serve the data to your end users" (read as IGDB's written authorization; the Agreement otherwise allows a 24-hour cache only). Re-syndication and redistribution of the data as the API gives it are prohibited (the Agreement). Attribution visible to the users, in a static place (not a changelog), to IGDB.com. Twitch client credentials (client id and secret) give the application token; never in a browser.

itch.io's server-side API documentation and terms (updated April 15 2023) state no rate limit and say nothing of commercial use, caching, storage or credit of its data. A game page's data.json needs no key; a player's ownership and library need an API key (the key option: a key generated in the account's settings reaches every endpoint, as a bearer token). The terms forbid harvesting or collecting information about others: a purchase looked up by e-mail address is for an address the site verified first.

attribution.text: Data from RAWG (rawg.io), with a link on every page that shows it

provenance.notes: Not read at the source: rawg.io, rawg.io/apidocs, rawg.io/tos_api and api.rawg.io all answered 522 (Cloudflare: the origin unreachable) on 2026-11-10. RAWG's own API description (its OpenAPI info, as APIs.guru mirrors it) asks every request to carry the key, the data and images credited to RAWG with an active hyperlink from every page that uses them, and "no cloning" of RAWG; it calls the API free for commercial use for projects of at most 100,000 monthly active users or 500,000 page views a month, larger ones writing to api@rawg.io - while search engines' copies of /apidocs give a free tier of 20,000 requests a month for non-commercial projects: limits and commercial use are not declared until read at the source.

attribution.text: Data from Steam; Valve, Steam and their logos are trademarks of Valve Corporation

provenance.notes: Limits and rights unknown: the Steam Web API Terms of Use (steamcommunity.com/dev/apiterms) and the Steam Subscriber Agreement could not be read on 2026-11-10 (the TLS handshake timed out from every client tried). Copies of the Web API terms indexed elsewhere limit a key to 100,000 calls a day; it is not declared until read at its source. The store's endpoints (appdetails, storesearch) are undocumented and publish no limit: about 200 requests per 5 minutes per IP is an unofficial figure (SteamDB, 2015), answered by 429 or 403 beyond it. The partner host (partner.steam-api.com, AuthenticateUserTicket with a publisher key) rate-limits the connecting IP after 403s, no figure given; publisher keys are never shipped in a game client. The store needs no key; a player's library and ownership need a Web API key (the key option), the identity check a publisher key. The attribution is the trademark line of Steamworks' branding guidelines (partner.steamgames.com/doc/marketing/branding, read on 2026-11-10).

Helix counts POINTS in a token bucket refilled every minute, one bucket for app access requests and one per user for user access requests; a request costs 1 point unless its endpoint says otherwise. The unit is points ("unit": "points"): a site that knows its bucket declares it, as Ratelimit-Limit says, e.g. {"max": 800, "window": "minute", "unit": "points", "cost": {"schedule": 2}} (schedule makes two requests, users and schedule; live one). Twitch's Ratelimit-Limit, Ratelimit-Remaining and Ratelimit-Reset headers are not the IETF fields; they are read as legacy fields, Ratelimit-Reset being "a Unix epoch timestamp" (the guide): no point left holds every call until the reset. A 429 is honoured. Developer Agreement (2024-12-04): Twitch content cached 24 hours at most and not shared, deleted items removed; re-syndicating or redistributing API data is prohibited, and Twitch data may not be sold, licensed or monetized absent a separate agreement; ads beside embeds only with other content of substantial value; a clear path to the source from every display, Twitch marks used only to attribute (twitch.tv/p/legal/trademark). Every request carries the Client-Id and an access token.

Not declared: the provider does not know the plan (a site declares its own with the policy option); Vimeo's X-RateLimit-* headers are not read, a 429 is. Developer Addendum (2026-03-09): charging users for the application needs Vimeo's written authorisation (3.5), no ads in the player without approval (3.4), Vimeo content stored or used only as the application's legitimate operation needs it, no data mining or datasets (4.1), no AI training (4.2), everything deleted at termination (8); no credit is asked, but nothing may imply Vimeo's endorsement and the Vimeo mark is used only descriptively (3.3).

Its CGU (last changed 14 May 2020): reuse of the data authorised, commercial included, "sans licence", provided the data's integrity is respected and the sources are cited as "Insee, BDM/{regroupement/dataflow}, date de l'extraction" (Series::$credit carries the series and the date); a link to the sources' documentation strongly recommended; 30 calls a minute; 99.5 % availability aimed at. insee.fr's legal notice puts its data under the Licence Ouverte 2.0 ("Source : Insee", the date of the data's last update). Caching is not addressed.

rateLimits.note: Production: 40 transactions a second per user, as Amadeus for Developers' rate-limits guide stated it (archived). The test environment allowed 10 a second, no more than one request every 100 ms: the provider gives that rate in place of this one when it is configured on the test environment. Amadeus counts HTTP requests, the guard counts calls: a search is a Hotel List request and up to one Hotel Search request per 20 hotels, an access token is one more request.

provenance.notes: Amadeus for Developers' Self-Service offer is gone: its developer guides were archived on 2026-07-17 ('[DEPRECATED] The Amadeus for Developers Self-Service offer has been deprecated'), the letter to its users (quoted by PhocusWire, 2026-02-09) said API keys would be disabled on July 17, test.api.amadeus.com no longer resolves, and the terms-of-service address now shows the cookies policy only. Amadeus says its Enterprise Portal and Enterprise APIs remain available, on contract (amadeus.com/en/contact). Production under Self-Service required signing its terms of service: commercial use is a contract. The terms themselves can no longer be read: caching, storage, redistribution, attribution and the data's licence are unknown. Card data in a booking falls under PCI DSS. Rate limits from the archived guide (docs/api-rate-limits.md); the monthly free quotas per API in test were never given as figures there.

No third party's terms: the site's own data. The listings are the site's, kept in its own store, reached with no network: no rate limit, no key, nothing to credit. What the hosts agreed to with the site (their listings shown, their calendars kept) is the site's business; a site may tighten this policy in its configuration (a limit on bookings a minute, for instance).

provenance.notes: No figure for the other functions: the API is under fair use and monitored; Billetweb asks to store the data on your side and read attendees incrementally (updatedSince), and any abuse, deliberate or not, may suspend the key. The key is a password: give it only to a trusted provider; a site stays responsible for what its AI agents do with it.

provenance.notes: Two figures for the hour: the API Terms of Use say 1,000 calls per OAuth token, the rate limits page 2,000 per application; both declared, the stricter counts. Each call counts one listing, not its pages (Eventbrite counts every request): a listing of several pages costs that many of Eventbrite's calls. Write actions (create, copy, publish an event, an event schedule) are 200 calls an hour each; this package only reads. Commercial use: no "direct commercial or monetary gain" from the APIs or the content, indirect gain supporting the application allowed, no competing product (3.6): the schema's one flag cannot hold that split, so unknown. Storage: only content about future events, none about past events without the user's permission (3.1), everything deleted within 30 days of termination (2.2) or when a user revokes consent (4.2): declared forbidden, the stricter form. Redistribution: no access to the stand-alone APIs (2.1). Attribution: listings show the event's title and a direct link to its Eventbrite page, without nofollow; the application uses its own name and says it is not Eventbrite's (3.2, 3.3). Limits may change at Eventbrite's discretion; a 429 holds the calls.

provenance.notes: Terms of Use last updated 2023-06-27. Commercial: "derive revenues from the use or provision of the Ticketmaster API, whether for direct commercial or monetary gain or otherwise" is forbidden "except as set forth below", and no exception follows (an affiliate agreement, if any, is a contract of its own: not read). Caching: Event Content may be cached or stored "for reasonable periods in order to provide the service", no time given: caching allowed, storage beyond it forbidden; content its owner asks to remove goes within 24 hours. Redistribution: the licence is non-sublicensable and non-transferable, the API may not be sold, leased or sublicensed. Calls not primarily in response to direct user actions may be rate limited or blocked. Each call counts one listing, not its pages; the Discovery API pages no deeper than the 1,000th result (as the package's docs read it on 2026-10-24; not re-read). The terms ask no attribution; the branding guide the Getting started page names answered 404 on 2026-11-10: attribution not declared. Over quota: 429, errorcode policies.ratelimit.QuotaViolation; the Rate-Limit, Rate-Limit-Available, Rate-Limit-Over and Rate-Limit-Reset headers are Ticketmaster's own, not read.

rateLimits.note: "more than 600 requests in the same minute will result in a 30 min ban" (fair use, per IP: the server's).
"more than 10 credentials attempts in the same minute, either valid or invalid, will result in a 1 min ban" (POST /auth/access_token).

provenance.notes: Legacy API (api.weezevent.com), access limited to registered Weezevent partners. Fair use: store what is read, filter queries (last_update for participants), keep the token on the server; Weezevent monitors calls and may limit or ban a key that does not use the API fairly. The limits are per IP and may change without notice. 5 invalid credentials in a row ban for 30 minutes (429): not a count the schema expresses. "token" is the provider's own access token request (username and password), guarded inside its operations (Config::guard()); a site giving access_token makes none. Each call counts one listing, not its pages. Commercial use, caching, redistribution and attribution: not addressed.

PayPal does not publish its rate limits: it may limit traffic that looks abusive and answers 429 RATE_LIMIT_REACHED (limits unknown, hence null). A PayPal help article advises fewer than 50 requests a minute to avoid an IP block: advice, not a published quota, so not declared. The OAuth token is kept for its lifetime (PayPal advises it). Creates carry PayPal-Request-Id when the caller gives an idempotency key.

rateLimits.note: The stricter form the schema can say. Shopify's real rule for the Admin GraphQL API is cost-based: a leaky bucket of query cost points restored at 100 points a second on the standard plans (200 Advanced, 1,000 Plus, 2,000 Commerce Components), each query at most 1,000 points, the bucket's state in every answer (extensions.cost.throttleStatus), which the provider's client reads and waits on. Two requests a second is the REST Admin API's leak rate on the standard plans.

provenance.notes: Limits per app and store. Not expressible in the schema: cost points per query (computed by Shopify per query and plan). Per store with 500,000 variants or more, 10,000 new variants a day (outside Shopify Plus); input arrays of 250 items at most; pagination up to 25,000 objects. Shopify documents no idempotency for draftOrderCreate: the provider never retries a mutation.

rateLimits.note: Stripe's global limit in a sandbox, and the default limit of each endpoint in both modes; live mode's global limit is 100 a second. One policy for both modes: the stricter is declared.
Connect account creations in a sandbox; 30 a second in live mode.

provenance.notes: Limits per account, per mode (docs.stripe.com/rate-limits, read 2026-11-10): global 100 requests a second live, 25 in a sandbox; 25 a second per endpoint unless noted; 1,000 updates an hour per PaymentIntent; Files 20 reads and 20 writes a second; Search 20 reads a second; Payouts 15 creations a second; Connect account creations 30 a second live, 5 in a sandbox; subscriptions 10 new invoices a minute and 20 a day each. Concurrency: 50 requests in flight in live mode by default, not published for sandboxes (not declared). Reads: on average no more than 500 per transaction over 30 days, at least 10,000 a month (not expressible: it depends on the transactions). A 429 carries Stripe-Rate-Limited-Reason; a 429 lock_timeout is not processed either. Writes carry the caller's Idempotency-Key. Use is governed by the Stripe Services Agreement (commercial, storage, redistribution: the contract's).

The REST API (wc/v3) sets no rate limit of its own: the shop is the merchant's own WordPress, and its host (a firewall, a security plugin, the hosting company) may limit it - a site adds that as its own tightening. WooCommerce's Store API rate limiting is opt-in and applies to the Store API only, which this provider does not call. The shop's data is the merchant's: redistribution depends on them.

Per feed: each network publishes its GTFS and GTFS-Realtime under its own licence and terms, so a feed's policy is the site's to give where it configures the feed - its licence (option licence: "ODbL-1.0", "etalab-2.0") and the credit its licence asks (option attribution), shown by Capabilities and Registry::policy(); a tightening (option policy: a GTFS-Realtime feed's rate limit, the licence's rights) on top. The static feed is read from the site's own store: no call is counted. A GTFS-Realtime feed's limits are its publisher's, unknown here.

Limits and rights unknown: navitia.io's terms page refused to be read on 2026-11-10 (HTTP 403), and SNCF's api.sncf.com publishes no quota. Copies of navitia.io's terms indexed elsewhere speak of a free tier of 5,000 requests a month, paid tiers above it and a credit to navitia.io with a link; Île-de-France Mobilités' own Navitia (PRIM) states 20,000 requests a day. None of this is declared until read at its source. The attribution option replaces the credit's text with what a coverage's data licence asks.

rateLimits.note: Transitous sets no hard cap: more than 720 requests in 24 hours of /plan (journeys), /one-to-many or /one-to-all is heavy use, to be agreed with the project first (its Matrix channel).

provenance.notes: For open-source, non-commercial projects light on resources; commercial use is not allowed (charities may ask for an exception). Every request names the application, its version and a contact in its User-Agent (a Referer in a browser). Link https://transitous.org/sources/ in a visible place, follow each source's conditions and OpenStreetMap's attribution guidelines. Caching and storage are not addressed: the project points to its dataset downloads rather than scraping the API.
